selected_blocks.text: We focus on the common binary setting of thinking versus no-thinking, which isolates the core routing–response credit-assignment problem from the separate design of multi-level reasoning budgets. For prompt xx, the policy first samples a mode m∼πθ(⋅∣x)m\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x), where TH\mathrm{TH} denotes thinking and NT\mathrm{NT} denotes no-thinking, and then generates a response z∼πθ(⋅∣x,m)z\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,m). We define the mode-conditioned value
Qθ(x,m)=𝔼z∼πθ(⋅∣x,m)[R(x,m,z)]Q_{\theta}(x,m)=\mathbb{E}_{z\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,m)}[R(x,m,z)] (1)
and the utility-optimal route under an efficiency margin b≥0b\geq 0:
mθ∗(x)=argmaxm∈{TH,NT}[Qθ(x,m)−b𝕀[m=TH]].m_{\theta}^{*}(x)=\arg\max_{m\in\{\mathrm{TH},\mathrm{NT}\}}\left[Q_{\theta}(x,m)-b\,\mathbb{I}[m=\mathrm{TH}]\right]. (2)

Ties are resolved in favor of NT\mathrm{NT}. The margin bb is a reward-space prior favoring the cheaper mode when estimated quality is similar; it is not a direct measurement of token or latency cost.

Let U(x,m,z)=R(x,m,z)−b𝕀[m=TH]U(x,m,z)=R(x,m,z)-b\,\mathbb{I}[m=\mathrm{TH}] be the efficiency-adjusted return and Q~θ(x,m)=𝔼[U∣x,m]\widetilde{Q}_{\theta}(x,m)=\mathbb{E}[U\mid x,m] its mode-conditioned value. Adding and subtracting Q~θ​(x,m)\widetilde{Q}_{\theta}(x,m) separates total return variation into two sources:

U−𝔼m′∼πθ(⋅∣x)[Q~θ(x,m′)]=\displaystyle U-\mathbb{E}_{m^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)}[\widetilde{Q}_{\theta}(x,m^{\prime})]={} Q~θ​(x,m)−𝔼m′​[Q~θ​(x,m′)]⏟between-mode routing credit\displaystyle\underbrace{\widetilde{Q}_{\theta}(x,m)-\mathbb{E}_{m^{\prime}}[\widetilde{Q}_{\theta}(x,m^{\prime})]}_{\text{between-mode routing credit}}
+U−Q~θ​(x,m)⏟within-mode response credit.\displaystyle+\underbrace{U-\widetilde{Q}_{\theta}(x,m)}_{\text{within-mode response credit}}. (3)

The first term evaluates the selected route against the current policy’s mode mixture; the second evaluates response quality within the selected mode. The expectation over modes is a conceptual baseline, not an additional learned critic. Equation 3 characterizes the hierarchical decision structure but does not prescribe adding and broadcasting the two terms across tokens. Instead, it suggests that routing and response decisions should receive different credit, while leaving open how these terms are estimated and optimized.

Based on the discussion and formulation above, self-routed training must estimate both modes’ current values, assign routing and response credit to the appropriate decisions, and preserve coverage of both modes as routing becomes autonomous. CounterRoute trains one shared policy πθ\pi_{\theta} with two complementary update types. A paired counterfactual update generates KK current-policy responses under each forced mode: cross-group reward comparisons train the routing token, while within-group GRPO trains subsequent response tokens. A self-routed update instead lets πθ\pi_{\theta} choose its mode and applies standard GRPO to the full generated sequence, including the routing token. A curriculum shifts training from paired supervision toward autonomous self-routing while retaining forced-mode coverage. Figure 2 gives an overview.

Paired updates provide balanced evidence for both routes and refresh routing targets as either response policy improves. Self-routed updates optimize the same parameters under the model’s own routing distribution, closing the online co-learning loop.
For each prompt xix_{i}, a paired counterfactual set contains two mode-specific GRPO groups, with KK rollouts per forced mode and 2​K2K rollouts in total:
yi,kTH\displaystyle y_{i,k}^{\text{TH}} ∼πθ(⋅∣xi,y1=tthink),k=1,…,K\displaystyle\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x_{i},y_{1}=t_{\text{think}}),\quad k=1,\ldots,K (4)
yi,kNT\displaystyle y_{i,k}^{\text{NT}} ∼πθ(⋅∣xi,y1=tnothink),k=1,…,K\displaystyle\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x_{i},y_{1}=t_{\text{nothink}}),\quad k=1,\ldots,K (5)

where tthink=<think>t_{\text{think}}=\texttt{<think>} and tnothink=</think>t_{\text{nothink}}=\texttt{</think>} are native vocabulary tokens. “Counterfactual” refers to intervening on the mode while holding the prompt and current policy parameters fixed. We prefill the selected token before generation and reorganize it to response position 0 afterward, so both groups expose the same routing position for training. Although prefilling controls generation, the reorganized token is treated as a response action and receives gradient at t=0t=0 rather than remaining part of the prompt context.
The per-prompt utility gap estimates the current benefit of thinking:

Δi=1K​∑k=1KR⁡(xi,yi,kTH)⏟mean reward (think)−1K​∑k=1KR⁡(xi,yi,kNT)⏟mean reward (no-think)−b\Delta_{i}=\underbrace{\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}R(x_{i},y_{i,k}^{\text{TH}})}_{\text{mean reward (think)}}-\underbrace{\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}R(x_{i},y_{i,k}^{\text{NT}})}_{\text{mean reward (no-think)}}-b (6)

Equation 6 is a Monte Carlo estimate of Q~θ​(xi,TH)−Q~θ​(xi,NT)\widetilde{Q}_{\theta}(x_{i},\mathrm{TH})-\widetilde{Q}_{\theta}(x_{i},\mathrm{NT}), the binary mode-value comparison implied by Eq. 2; its sign therefore identifies the preferred route. Pairing the estimates within each prompt controls for prompt difficulty while refreshing the target under the current policy. Here R∈[0,1]R\in[0,1] is the task reward and b≥0b\geq 0 is an asymmetric margin favoring no-think when the modes achieve similar reward. We use a scheduled bb-decay: bb is larger early (e.g., b=0.05b=0.05) to overcome the initial thinking preference, then reduced, potentially to zero, once both modes are established. The margin affects only routing credit and is not subtracted from within-group response rewards. It is a reward-space margin rather than a measured token or latency cost; Appendix D.3 reports fixed-margin controls and a checkpoint after the scheduled bb-decay has completed.

CounterRoute uses the hierarchical decomposition in Eq. 3 to motivate decision-aligned credit assignment. Let m∈{TH,NT}m\in\{\mathrm{TH},\mathrm{NT}\} index the mode, k∈{1,…,K}k\in\{1,\ldots,K\} a rollout within its group, and tt the response position, with σTH=+1\sigma_{\mathrm{TH}}=+1 and σNT=−1\sigma_{\mathrm{NT}}=-1. Let A^i,m,kGRPO\widehat{A}^{\mathrm{GRPO}}_{i,m,k} denote the reward advantage normalized among the KK responses in the same mode-specific group. For paired updates, CounterRoute assigns

A^i,m,k,t={σm​s​tanh⁡(Δi),t=0(routing token),A^i,m,kGRPO,t≥1(response tokens).\widehat{A}_{i,m,k,t}=\begin{cases}\sigma_{m}s\tanh(\Delta_{i}),&t=0\quad\text{(routing token)},\\ \widehat{A}^{\mathrm{GRPO}}_{i,m,k},&t\geq 1\quad\text{(response tokens)}.\end{cases} (7)

The original GRPO advantage at position 0 is overwritten by signed cross-group credit. The tanh\tanh bounds it to [−s,+s][-s,+s], allowing the routing update to flow through the standard actor objective without a separate router head:
∇θJroute=𝔼⁡[∑i,m,kA^i,m,k,0​∇θ​log⁡πθ​(tm∣xi)].\nabla_{\theta}J_{\text{route}}=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i,m,k}\widehat{A}_{i,m,k,0}\,\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(t_{m}\mid x_{i})\right]. (8)

For Δi>0\Delta_{i}>0, the think token receives positive routing credit and the no-think token receives negative credit; the signs reverse when Δi<0\Delta_{i}<0. Because the two tokens compete in the same position-0 softmax, this shifts their log-odds toward the preferred mode. Under token-mean aggregation, the two position-0 terms share the same global denominator and receive symmetric loss weighting despite different response lengths, although their parameter gradients still depend on token probabilities. Since the route tokens are intervened rather than sampled, this is a balanced intervention-based surrogate, not an unbiased gradient under the naturally sampled route distribution.

Let Gi,m,kG_{i,m,k} denote the scalar response reward used by standard GRPO and G¯i,m=K−1​∑kGi,m,k\bar{G}_{i,m}=K^{-1}\sum_{k}G_{i,m,k}. Omitting standard numerical stabilization, the within-group response advantage is
A^i,m,kGRPO=Gi,m,k−G¯i,mStdk′∈[K]⁡[Gi,m,k′].\widehat{A}^{\mathrm{GRPO}}_{i,m,k}=\frac{G_{i,m,k}-\bar{G}_{i,m}}{\operatorname{Std}_{k^{\prime}\in[K]}\!\left[G_{i,m,k^{\prime}}\right]}. (9)

For t≥1t\geq 1, the second line of Eq. 7 applies this advantage only to subsequent response tokens. Separate mode-specific groups preserve the ranking among responses generated under the same route despite the modes’ different length and reward distributions. Thus paired updates use cross-group comparison for the routing token and within-group GRPO for response tokens; the disjoint signals still update the same shared parameters.

For each self-routed (SR) prompt, KK complete responses are sampled as yi,kSR∼πθ(⋅∣xi)y_{i,k}^{\mathrm{SR}}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x_{i}), including the position-0 routing token. Standard GRPO then trains the full generated sequence. Position 0 therefore retains its ordinary GRPO advantage rather than receiving the paired counterfactual overwrite. These updates optimize responses under the model’s learned route distribution and allow autonomous routing itself to keep adapting.

Direct self-routing from initialization can reinforce the initial mode preference before the alternative mode receives useful feedback. CounterRoute therefore begins with paired coverage and gradually increases the self-routed fraction. At steady state, 70% of prompt slots use self-routed updates and 30% use paired updates, preserving counterfactual supervision while transferring most training to autonomous routing. Full milestones are in Appendix C.

With paired ratio ρ\rho, the per-step rollout multiplier vs. a same-data GRPO baseline is 1+ρ1+\rho: 2.0×\times initially, declining to 1.3×\times at steady state (70% SR + 30% paired). The cost is a transient warm-up premium, not a recurring 2×\times. CounterRoute requires no method-specific SFT stage beyond the dual-mode Qwen3 initialization.
